brief.situation: You are the clinical informatics project lead at Cedar Valley Clinics (fictional), six primary care clinics moving to a new ambulatory EHR. Go-live is set for day 28, and the steering committee holds the go/no-go meeting on day 21. Three things are open: 6% of test prescriptions fail to reach pharmacies, the converted allergy and medication lists have not been checked against the old system, and 61% of clinicians have finished training.
handover: The go-live budget left is 400 thousand dollars. Each extra week of the old and new systems running side by side costs about 60 thousand.
The chief medical officer wants clinicians safe and supported; the chief financial officer wants the date kept.
howItWorks: The clock runs in days: each task takes days. Choose it, then let it finish, which moves the calendar on.
The board shows the readiness risks against the appetite, each executive's support in words, the budget committed and the docket.
After go-live, close the project and write the readiness record.

writeup.question: For the steering committee: how you decided when to go live, what had to be true first, and how the change will stick.

parts.label: Deciding
parts.criteria: Measurable go-live criteria agreed before the go/no-go meeting; the criteria, not the calendar or a vendor, decide; a bounded slip when they are not met rather than an open-ended postponement.
parts.modelAnswer: No severity-1 open, conversion validated, 90% trained, command center ready; go when met, up to two weeks to meet them.

parts.label: What had to be true
parts.criteria: The prescription defect fixed and retested end to end (testing); the converted allergy lists validated by sampling against the old system (a patient safety check); training finished with access tied to it; a command center, super-users and the downtime plan (contingency).
parts.modelAnswer: 0 of 400 test prescriptions failing; 3% allergy error found and reloaded; 94% trained; command center staffed.

parts.label: Sustaining
parts.criteria: Go-live is a step in the life cycle, not its end: optimization with usage reports, workflow fixes and refresher training after go-live.
parts.modelAnswer: A 30-day optimization with weekly usage reports and fixes.

live.headline: Good: the criteria decided
live.body: Measured criteria agreed in advance turned a date fight into a checklist. The defect was retested end to end, the conversion was validated against the old system before anyone relied on it, clinicians were trained with access tied to training, and support and optimization carried the change past go-live.

costly.headline: Live, at a cost
costly.body: No unsafe defect reached the clinics, but something in the life cycle was skipped: criteria agreed after the call, go-live without full training or support, or no plan to sustain the change.

unsafe.headline: Live with a known safety defect
unsafe.body: A failing prescription interface and unvalidated allergy lists are patient safety problems, not post-go-live tasks. Test end to end and validate converted clinical data before go-live.

overspend.headline: Over budget
overspend.body: Postponing without criteria keeps two systems running and fixes nothing faster. A bounded slip tied to named criteria costs far less.

time_up.headline: Time up
time_up.body: No readiness record was written before the case's limit.

scoring.modelReasoning: Go-live is a step in the EHR life cycle, not its finish line, and the go/no-go call should rest on criteria agreed in advance. Here those are no open severity-1 defect, validated conversion, 90% of clinicians trained with access tied to training, and a command center with the downtime plan rehearsed. The prescription defect needs the vendor's fix and an end-to-end retest; the converted allergy lists need sampling against the old system, which finds a 3% mapping error to fix before anyone relies on them. Go when the criteria are met, with a bounded slip if not, then sustain the change with usage reports, workflow fixes and refreshers.
